# Recovery of Left Ventricular Systolic Function and Clinical Outcomes in Young Adults With Myocardial Infarction

**Authors:** Wanda Y. Wu; David W. Biery; Avinainder Singh; Sanjay Divakaran; Adam N. Berman; Gloria Ayuba; Ersilia M. DeFilippis; Khurram Nasir; James L. Januzzi; Marcelo F. Di Carli; Deepak L. Bhatt; Ron Blankstein

**Affiliations:** aCardiovascular Division, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts; | bBoston University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts; | cYale University School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut; | dNewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, New York; | eHouston Methodist Hospital, Houston, Texas; | fCardiology Division, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts; | gDepartment of Radiology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts.

## Abstract

Left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) recovery is associated with better long-term outcomes after myocardial infarction (MI). However, the association between long-term outcomes and EF recovery among young MI patients has not been investigated.

The study sought to evaluate the prevalence of left ventricular systolic dysfunction among patients who experience their first MI at a young age and compare outcomes between those who recovered their EF versus those who did not.

The YOUNG-MI registry is a retrospective cohort study of patients who experienced an MI at ≤50 years of age. EF at the time of MI and within 180 days post-MI were determined from all available medical records. The primary outcomes were all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

There were 1,724 patients with baseline EF data: 503 (29%) had EF <50%, whereas 1,221 (71%) had a normal baseline EF. Patients with lower EF were more likely to have experienced ST-segment elevation MI, have higher troponin values, and have more severe angiographic coronary artery disease. Among patients with abnormal baseline EF, information on follow-up EF was available for 216, of whom 90 (42%) recovered their EF to ≥50%. Patients who experienced EF recovery had less severe angiographic disease, lower alcohol use, and a lower burden of comorbidities. Over a median follow-up of 11.1 years, EF recovery was associated with an ~8-fold reduction in all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.12; p = 0.001) and a ~10-fold reduction in cardiovascular mortality (adjusted hazard ratio: 0.10; p = 0.025).

Nearly one-third of young patients presented with left ventricular dysfunction post-MI. Among them, EF recovery occurred in more than 40% and was independently associated with a substantial decrease in all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.

Left ventricular ejection fraction (EF) is a widely used prognostic tool to identify patients at risk of adverse cardiovascular (CV) events and increased mortality following acute myocardial infarction (MI) (1–4). As such, the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines recommend assessment of left ventricular systolic function for all patients admitted with acute MI (5,6). However, a number of studies have demonstrated that a significant percentage of MI patients with reduced baseline EF can recover their EF over time (7–10), and such recovery is associated with a lower risk of long-term CV events (11–14). Conversely, patients who do not experience EF recovery post-MI have a higher risk of adverse remodeling, sudden cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, and CV and all-cause mortality, independent of revascularization, medical therapy, peak troponin, and baseline EF (11–14).

Although previous studies have consistently demonstrated better prognosis for post-MI patients with improved or fully recovered EF, these studies have included older patient populations with median ages ranging from 60 to 66 years old (11–14). As such, the frequency of EF recovery and its association with long-term outcomes have not been well studied in younger patients who experience an MI.

Given that MI rates in young adults have not declined as they have for older individuals (15–17), and that the risk factors and prognosis of young MI patients may be different from those of their older counterparts (17–19), it is imperative to understand the benefits of EF recovery in this population. Therefore, we sought to evaluate the incidence of left ventricular dysfunction among patients who experienced a first MI at ≤50 years of age and to test the hypothesis that patients who recover their EF post-MI have improved clinical outcomes when compared with those who have a persistently reduced EF.

## METHODS

### STUDY POPULATION.

The design of the YOUNG-MI registry has been previously described (20). In short, this is a retrospective cohort study from 2 large academic medical centers (Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Massachusetts General Hospital) that included patients who experienced their first MI at ≤50 years of age between the years of 2000 and 2016. All medical records were adjudicated by a team of study physicians, as previously described (20) using the Third Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (21). For the present analysis, only patients who experienced a type 1 MI on index admission were included, while individuals with known coronary artery disease (CAD) (defined as a prior MI or revascularization) were excluded. The YOUNG-MI registry has been approved by the Institutional Review Board at Partners HealthCare.

### RISK FACTORS.

A detailed review of electronic health records was conducted to determine the presence of baseline CV risk factors. Diabetes was defined as fasting plasma glucose >126 mg/dl, hemoglobin A1c ≥6.5%, or diagnosis or treatment of diabetes. Hypertension was defined as systolic blood pressure ≥140 mm Hg, diastolic blood pressure ≥90 mm Hg, or diagnosis or treatment of hypertension. Dyslipidemia was defined as total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dl, serum triglycerides ≥150 mg/dl, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol <40 mg/dl in men or <50 mg/dl in women, or diagnosis or treatment of dyslipidemia. Obesity was defined as a body mass index ≥30 kg/m2 or a diagnosis of obesity. Current smoking was defined as using tobacco products within the last month. Family history of pre-mature CAD was defined as fatal MI, nonfatal MI, or coronary revascularization occurring before 55 years of age in first-degree male family members and before 65 years of age in first-degree female family members, and was determined by a review of electronic medical records. Alcohol use was defined as having a positive toxicology report for alcohol during the index hospitalization or a documented diagnosis or treatment of alcohol use. Illicit substance use was defined as having a positive toxicology report during the index hospitalization for 1 or more of marijuana, cocaine, heroin, or methamphetamines, or a documented diagnosis or treatment for use of these substances.

In order to adjust for comorbidities, the Charlson Comorbidity Index, a method of predicting the risk of mortality based on comorbidities, was calculated for each patient as determined by International Classification of Diseases–Ninth Revision diagnosis and billing codes associated with the index hospitalization (22). Additionally, because lower socioeconomic status is known to be associated with all-cause mortality, household income for each patient was estimated based on household zip codes (23).

### LABORATORY VALUES.

Peak troponin was defined as the highest measured troponin value (bounded at 500 ng/mL to minimize bias from outliers), standardized through natural logarithm transform.

### BASELINE AND FOLLOW-UP EFs.

Baseline and follow-up EF data were ascertained for each individual through comprehensive review of transthoracic echocardiogram reports. However, when data from transthoracic echocardiography were not available, EF data recorded from the following imaging modalities were also included: cardiac magnetic resonance, single-photon emission computed tomography, positron emission tomography, ventriculography during cardiac catheterization, and cardiac computed tomography. When tests were visually interpreted as having hyperdynamic EF, an EF of 70% was recorded. When tests were visually interpreted as having normal EF, an EF of 60% was recorded. Patients with a baseline EF were stratified into 2 groups according to the following categories: abnormal (EF <50%) or normal (EF ≥50%). Baseline EF was defined as the EF value closest to index MI up to 7 days post-MI. All EF values from all modalities were recorded up until 13 months after the date of index MI. The follow-up EF for each patient was determined by selecting the EF closest to 10 weeks, occurring any time after 2 weeks but within 6 months post-MI. This time range was selected based on prior data showing that EF recovery based on repeat EF measurements beyond 6 weeks was a stronger predictor of future cardiac arrest and all-cause mortality than EF measurements at <2 weeks (11). Earlier EF measurements may reflect the effects of myocardial stunning, and are less likely to account for future adverse remodeling or subsequent fibrosis (24,25).

### CRITERIA FOR EF RECOVERY.

Patients with an abnormal baseline EF and available follow-up EF were further stratified based on whether or not they achieved absolute EF recovery, defined as achieving an EF ≥50%, within 6 months post-MI. In addition, in a sensitivity analysis, we tested 4 alternative criteria for EF recovery: 1) modest improvement (ΔEF ≥5%); 2) considerable improvement (ΔEF ≥10%); 3) modest improvement or absolute recovery (ΔEF ≥5% or follow-up EF ≥50%); and 4) considerable improvement or absolute recovery (ΔEF ≥10% or follow-up EF ≥50%).

### ANGIOGRAPHIC FINDINGS.

Invasive angiographic findings were ascertained through a review of all available cardiac catheterization images by a single interventional cardiologist blinded to all patient outcomes and risk factors. Both culprit lesions and nonculprit lesions were identified. For each lesion, the location and severity of stenosis (as assessed visually, and ranging from 20% to 100%) were classified according to the modified American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology lesion classification scheme (26).

Two different measures were used to determine the extent and severity of coronary artery plaque. A segment involvement score (SIS) was employed as a measure of plaque extent, and was calculated as the total number of coronary artery segments exhibiting plaque, irrespective of the degree of luminal stenosis within each segment. For each patient, the SIS ranged from a minimum of 0 to a maximum of 16 (27). In addition, the Gensini score was used as a method of quantifying the overall severity of coronary stenosis while accounting for lesion location, as previously described (28).

### OUTCOMES.

The primary outcomes of interest were all-cause death and CV death. Vital status was assessed by the Social Security Administration Death Master File, the Massachusetts Department of Vital Statistics, and the National Death Index. Cause of death was adjudicated independently by 2 cardiologists. Cases in which there was disagreement were reviewed by an adjudication committee, with decisions reached by consensus. Death was classified as CV or non-CV death, as per published criteria (20,29). If death certificates were not available, deaths were conservatively classified as non-CV. Causes of CV deaths included acute MI, heart failure, sudden cardiac death, ischemic stroke, nontraumatic hemorrhagic stroke, immediate complications of a CV procedure, CV hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, and peripheral artery disease (29).

### STATISTICAL ANALYSIS.

All analyses were performed using Stata version 15.1 (StataCorp, College Station, Texas). Categorical variables are reported as frequencies and proportions, and compared with chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. Continuous variables were reported as means or medians and compared with t tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, as appropriate. The proportional hazards assumption was assessed by analyzing the Schoenfeld residuals. Survival curves for all-cause and CV mortality were compared using the log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards modeling was used to assess the prognostic capability of baseline EF as well as all the different criteria used to determine EF recovery. Multivariate Cox models incorporated adjustment for all baseline covariates that had a significant (p ≤ 0.05) univariate association with the outcome being investigated and for variables that have a known association with mortality. The multivariate predictors model for EF recovery incorporated adjustment for all baseline covariates that had a significant (p ≤ 0.05) univariate association with EF recovery, and also included coronary revascularization and medications that have a known association with EF recovery. Kaplan-Meier time-to-event curves were constructed to illustrate the cumulative incidence of both clinical endpoints. For all survival analyses, we excluded patients with a positive human immunodeficiency virus status or who were documented as having any oncological malignancy in order to avoid possible competing non-CV hazards.

## RESULTS

### BASELINE EF.

#### Baseline characteristics.

Of the 2,097 patients who experienced an MI at a young age, 1,724 (82%) had an EF measured at the time of their index MI. Among those with a baseline EF, 503 (29%) had an abnormal EF (mean EF 39%), while 1,221 (71%) had a normal EF (mean EF 60%), as depicted in Figure 1. The mean age at time of MI (44 ± 5.1 years) and sex distribution were similar between the 2 groups. Patients with abnormal baseline EF were more likely to have experienced an ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI), have higher troponin values, have more severe angiographic CAD (as determined by the Gensini score), have diabetes, and be white. In addition, patients with abnormal baseline EF were more likely to undergo coronary revascularization, and were more likely to be treated with coronary artery bypass grafting. A full comparison of baseline characteristics between these 2 groups is listed in Tables 1 and 2.

#### All-cause mortality.

Among patients with a baseline EF, there were 6 (0.005%) deaths in those with a normal baseline EF and 22 (0.040%) deaths in those with an abnormal baseline EF. The annual death rate post-discharge among those with a normal baseline EF was 0.73 deaths per 100 person-years, whereas that of those with an abnormal baseline EF was 1.73 deaths per 100 person-years (p < 0.001). When compared with patients who had an abnormal baseline EF, the univariate hazard ratio (HR) for all-cause mortality in those with a normal baseline EF was 0.46 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.34 to 0.62; p < 0.001). After adjusting for age; sex; income; length of stay; hypertension; diabetes; alcohol use; drug use; presence and duration of angina; peripheral vascular disease; Charlson Comorbidity Index; high-density lipoprotein cholesterol; triglycerides; estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR); coronary revascularization; SIS; prescription of a statin, beta-blocker, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor, or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) on discharge; and statin intensity, the HR was no longer significant (HR: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.66 to 1.45; p = 0.906).

#### Cardiovascular mortality.

Similar results were observed for CV mortality. The CV death rate among patients with a normal baseline EF was 0.31 deaths per 100 person-years, while that of patients with an abnormal baseline EF was 1.02 deaths per 100 person-years (p < 0.001). When compared with patients who had an abnormal baseline EF, the univariate HR for CV mortality in those with a normal baseline EF was 0.31 (95% CI: 0.20 to 0.48; p < 0.001). After adjusting for age; sex; income; length of stay; hypertension; diabetes; obesity; alcohol use; drug use; presence and duration of angina; peripheral arterial disease; Charlson Comorbidity Index; eGFR; coronary revascularization; SIS; prescription of a statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, or ARB on discharge; and statin intensity, the HR was no longer significant (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.47 to 1.39; p = 0.442).

### EF RECOVERY.

#### Baseline characteristics.

Among the 503 patients who had an abnormal baseline EF, 216 (43%) had available data on follow-up EF within the prespecified time period. Patients with follow-up EF data had similar risk factor profiles, baseline EF, and all-cause and CV mortality as those without follow-up data with the exception that those with available data on follow-up EF were more likely to have experienced a STEMI (Supplemental Table 1). Among patients who had data on follow-up EF, the mean time between baseline EF measurements and follow-up EF measurements was 68 ± 44 days.

When considering patients with an abnormal baseline EF and available follow-up, 90 (42%) experienced absolute EF recovery (≥50%) whereas 126 (58%) did not experience such recovery. When comparing the baseline characteristics between patients with and without EF recovery, there were no significant differences in age, sex, or most major CV risk factors. However, patients who did not recover their EF were more likely to use alcohol and had more severe angiographic CAD, as determined by the Gensini score. Interestingly, there was no significant difference in EF recovery between patients who presented with STEMI versus those who presented with non-STEMI (p = 0.240). A full comparison of baseline characteristics between these 2 groups can be found in Tables 3 and 4.

With respect to the 4 alternative criteria of recovery, of the 216 patients who had an abnormal baseline EF and available follow-up within the prespecified time period, the numbers of patients who recovered in each alternative recovery criterion were 136 (63.0%), 98 (45.4%), 139 (64.4%), and 111 (51.4%) for alternative criteria groups 1 to 4, respectively (Table 5).

In addition, as expected, a higher baseline EF was independently associated with a follow-up EF that recovered to ≥50% (p < 0.001); however, baseline EF was not associated with an EF increase of ≥5% (p = 0.36).

#### All-cause mortality.

Of the 216 patients with an abnormal baseline EF and available follow-up between 2 weeks and 6 months post-MI, there were 4 (4.4%) deaths among the patients who recovered their EF to ≥50% and 32 (25.4%) deaths among patients who did not experience such recovery (p < 0.001) over a median follow-up of 11.1 (interquartile range: 7.1 to 14.1) years. The annual death rate post-discharge among those who recovered their EF to ≥50% was 0.46 deaths per 100 person-years, while that of those who did not recover their EF to ≥50% was 2.67 deaths per 100 person-years (p < 0.001). There was an approximately 5-fold decrease in all-cause mortality for patients in this recovery group (univariate HR: 0.19; 95% CI: 0.07 to 0.56; p = 0.002). After adjusting for age, sex, baseline EF, income, STEMI, diabetes mellitus, presence and type of coronary revascularization, prescription of a P2Y12 inhibitor or statin on discharge, and statin intensity, the HR remained significant (HR: 0.12; 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.40; p = 0.001) (Figure 2A). Both the univariate and adjusted HRs for all-cause mortality for the 4 alternative recovery criteria tested in our sensitivity analysis also remained highly significant (Table 5).

#### Cardiovascular mortality.

In the same 216 patients with an abnormal baseline EF, there were 2 (2.2%) CV deaths among patients who recovered their EF to ≥50% and 14 (11.1%) CV deaths among those who did not (p = 0.016). The CV death rate among patients who recovered their EF to ≥50% was 0.23 deaths per 100 person-years, whereas that of patients who did not was 1.34 deaths per 100 person-years (p = 0.11). The univariate HR for CV mortality in patients with abnormal baseline EF who recovered their EF to ≥50% was 0.23 (95% CI: 0.05 to 1.02; p = 0.053), which trended toward significance. After adjusting for age; sex; baseline EF; diabetes mellitus; Charlson Comorbidity Index; presence and type of coronary revascularization; eGFR; prescription of a statin, P2Y12 inhibitor, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, or ARB on discharge; and statin intensity, the HR was significant (HR: 0.10; 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.75; p = 0.025) (Figure 2B).

Among the 4 alternative criteria for recovery tested in our sensitivity analysis, only patients who experienced recovery criterion 3 (i.e., absolute recovery [$50%] or improvement of their EF of ≥5%) had a significant reduction in CV events on both the univariate (HR: 0.32; p = 0.048) and multivariate (HR: 0.18, p = 0.023) models. The unadjusted and adjusted HRs for CV mortality for each of the alternative criteria tested are shown in Table 5.

#### Predictors of absolute recovery.

Among patients with an abnormal baseline EF, 6 variables were associated with absolute EF recovery on a univariate basis: Gensini score (odds ratio [OR]: 0.99; p = 0.002), length of stay (OR: 0.91; p = 0.009), alcohol use (OR: 0.32; p = 0.017), peak troponin (OR: 0.83, p = 0.039), percutaneous coronary intervention (OR: 1.29; p = 0.049), and baseline EF (OR: 1.15; p < 0.001). Predictors of absolute recovery on a multivariate basis included Gensini score (OR: 0.99; p = 0.010), length of stay (OR: 0.89; p = 0.018), alcohol use (OR: 0.27; p = 0.023), peak troponin (OR: 0.78; p = 0.040), baseline EF (OR: 1.11; p < 0.001), and coronary artery bypass grafting (OR: 10.15; p = 0.021) (Supplemental Table 2)

## DISCUSSION

Our study, the first to evaluate the impact of EF recovery among young patients post-MI, showed that EF recovery within 6 months post-MI was associated with a significant reduction in long-term all-cause death and CV death. Importantly, nearly 30% of young patients who experienced acute MI at a young age had abnormal baseline EF, and only 42% of them experienced EF recovery to ≥50%. Among these young patients who did not recover their EF, there was a staggering 25.4% mortality rate over a follow-up period of 11.1 years. Patients who experienced EF recovery had less severe angiographic disease, shorter hospital stay, less alcohol use, and smaller infarct size. There was a similar proportion of diabetic patients who recovered their EF versus those who did not, suggesting that diabetes did not significantly affect EF recovery. Diuretic use was higher in patients who did not experience EF recovery, likely reflecting the fact that diuretic use was a marker of heart failure. Interestingly, prescription of medical therapies that improve EF, such as beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and ARBs, was not significantly associated with EF recovery. Our findings support measuring serial EFs for determining prognosis among young MI patients who are found to have a reduced EF upon admission. In addition, our findings emphasize the importance of implementing therapies that have been shown to improve EF and outcomes post-MI.

Additionally, patients with abnormal baseline EF were more likely to have experienced a STEMI, have larger infarcts, have diabetes, have more severe angiographic CAD, and undergo coronary revascularization. Interestingly, reduced baseline EF alone was not associated with higher rates of all-cause or CV death after adjusting for significant baseline risk factors, coronary revascularization, extent of CAD, and use of medical therapy. This implies that EF recovery is a significant predictor of long-term prognosis after acute MI.

Although the mean age in our study was 44 years, prior studies have also shown that EF recovery is associated with better long-term outcomes post-MI among older cohorts with median age between 60 and 70 years (11–14). Chew et al. (11) found that older patients who experienced EF recovery to >40% had a 4-fold lower risk of future adverse events and all-cause and CV mortality when compared with patients who did not recover. Similarly, the REFINE (Risk Estimation Following Infarction Non-invasive Evaluation) study showed that patients who experienced EF recovery had decreased rates of cardiac death and resuscitated cardiac arrest (13). Last, Parodi et al. (14) determined that post-MI patients who recovered their EF had significantly lower 5-year cardiac mortality rates, lower 5-year hospitalization rates for heart failure, and lower rates of left ventricular remodeling within 6 months post-MI.

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to explore the long-term benefits of EF recovery in young patients post-MI, specifically patients ≤50 years of age. Exploring younger populations may be important, as they often have different etiologies and risk factors for their MI (17,18,30–33). In addition, MI rates in the young have not decreased as they have for older cohorts (15–17); thus, it is likely that clinicians will encounter a larger proportion of young MI patients in the future.

### CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS.

Although the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association guidelines recommend that all patients admitted with acute MI should have evaluation of their baseline EF (class 1 recommendation), guidelines are less clear in regard to when EF should be reassessed in the months after an MI (5,6). Our study suggests that in post-MI patients, EF reassessed at >2 weeks, but <6 months, can give valuable information on long-term prognosis, outcomes, and potential ongoing need for medical therapy. It also reemphasizes the importance of early and assiduous application of guideline-directed medical therapies with favorable effects on adverse remodeling (e.g., ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or beta-blockers) in this setting in order to achieve best outcomes.

### STUDY LIMITATIONS.

Our study was limited by its retrospective nature. However, this study design is well suited for studying less frequent medical conditions such as MI in the young. We estimate that a similar prospective study would have required at least 10 years to allow for the recruitment of the same number of patients. There are also inherent limitations regarding the assessment of EF when using echocardiography. For instance, visual estimation of EF may vary by interpreter or by institution (34), with a coefficient of variation for left ventricular systolic function as high as 15% (35). However, echocardiography, compared with other imaging modalities, has been shown to provide an accurate estimation of EF and is widely used in clinical research (36–38). Another limitation is that <50% of patients with an abnormal baseline EF had at least 1 follow-up EF within the prespecified time period. However, patients with and without follow-up EF had similar risk factors profiles, baseline EF, and rates of all-cause and CV mortality (Supplemental Table 1). Last, some studies have shown an association between EF recovery and several clinical variables such as female sex, presence of beta-blocker therapy, and faster door-to-balloon time (11,14,39–41). Although we identified 6 independent predictors of EF recovery, it remains possible that we were underpowered to detect additional ones.

Some studies have indicated that aspirin use may increase B-type natriuretic peptide levels in patients who are coadministered ACE inhibitors, as aspirin may interact with an ACE inhibitor’s ability to prevent structural remodeling (42,43). Because aspirin was prescribed for the vast majority of our post-MI cohort, it is possible that its use attenuated the magnitude of EF recovery. Despite these limitations, our study also has several noteworthy strengths. We evaluated one of the largest cohorts of patients who experienced an MI at a young age, and our study is the first to examine the association between EF recovery and long-term outcomes among younger individuals. Our findings that young patients who recovered their EF had reduced rates of all-cause mortality remained robust even when considering all alternative criteria for EF recovery. In addition, this study had a median follow-up period of 11.1 years, which allowed us to explore long-term outcomes. Last, all patient records, including risk factors and outcomes, were adjudicated by study physicians, which is a more accurate method that other studies that have relied on billing data.

## CONCLUSIONS

Approximately one-third of young patients presented with left ventricular systolic dysfunction after acute MI. However, a significant percentage of them recover their EF to ≥50%, and such recovery was associated with a substantial decrease in all-cause and CV mortality. Our findings suggest the need to reassess EF among young patients with a baseline EF <50%, especially given the implications on long-term prognosis and management.
